title: A Compendium of the Record of Responses and Retribution (Original Text)
excerpt: A Compendium of Commentaries, Lectures, and Case Records on the Taishang Record of Responses and Retribution (Volume One)

blocks.text: Preface One to the Compendium of the Record of Responses and Retribution

inline.s: This treatise takes its name from the two words response and retribution. Response is the cause; retribution is the effect. Its opening four lines read: “Calamity and blessing have no gate; man brings them on himself. The recompense of good and evil follows like a shadow.” They set forth the principle of cause and effect, that doing good brings blessing and doing evil brings calamity, most simply and most clearly. If a person can understand the principle of cause and effect, and knows that doing evil must bring disaster, then even if he were forced to do evil, his heart would surely hold some fear and he would not dare to comply. Knowing that doing good must bring blessing and emolument, his heart likewise has something it seeks, and even if others hindered his good deeds he would not be willing to stop.

Master Yinguang once said: Cause and effect is the great authority by which the sages of the world and beyond the world pacify the world and liberate living beings. In this present age, if one does not promote the principle of cause and effect and of the round of birth and death, then even were all the Buddhas, patriarchs, and sages to appear together, they could not bring it about that the world be at peace and the people happy.

Although the Record of Responses comes from the Daoist canon, its annotations draw heavily upon Confucian books and Buddhist sutras, so that by reading one book one gains the essential meaning of the three teachings. That is the first joy. The Compendium gathers the various annotated editions of past and present, examines and selects them with care, refining upon refinement, and so compiles them into a single book; thus in reading the one book of the Compendium one has read every annotated edition of the Record of Responses. That is the second joy. The editor’s eye and hand rise above all his peers, and none can compare with him. The reader who obtains this good guide finds his measure of mind opened wide by it and his seeds of blessing broadly planted by it. That is the third joy. The highest principles and famous sayings of the Confucian teaching, its work of sincerity and rectification, its essential methods of cultivating the self and ordering the family — this compilation has already gathered more than half of them. The textual prajñā of the Buddhist gate may here too be glimpsed in part. And the essential meaning of the Daoist art of gathering in the mind has likewise been assembled here. That is the fourth joy. Therefore the Compendium is not only the king of all annotations on the Record of Responses; it is in truth the king of all books of goodness. Whoever encounters it is a person of blessing. Whoever can read it straight through to the end, calming the mind and settling the breath, turning it over and savoring it again and again, embodying it within and putting it into practice in his affairs — that is a person of great blessing. And if he seeks further into its refinements, then becoming a sage or worthy, becoming a Buddha or patriarch, lies wholly within it. To live in this world and be unable to see this king of books, but to sink and drift through long kalpas with no way to pull oneself free — is that not a great misfortune? The annotations of the Record of Responses are so clear, so detailed, so penetrating, so earnest — no less than one who pulls your ear and instructs you to your face, no less than one who cries out with a loud voice; and the compassion in that breast is such that tears fall with the words. One who has the affinity to read this should of course turn back. Why doubt it?

This treatise comprises two hundred ninety-three sayings. The good and evil it records are complete in both great and small. I earnestly pray that all people will diligently uphold this treatise. One must at every moment recite it silently in the mind, so that every word turns back into one’s own person: Have I this fault or not? Gradually let them grow few. Day after day thus, year after year thus, and naturally wherever one moves there is good, wherever one touches there is good. One may of oneself leave suffering and attain joy, have blessing and no calamity, have auspiciousness and no misfortune.
May 1959
Respectfully recorded on the occasion of the reprinting by Lin Xia’an of Foshan

blocks.text: Preface Two to the Compendium of the Record of Responses and Retribution

inline.s: The heart of Heaven and Earth is a heart of utter goodness. Human beings, born within the transformations of qi, are by nature all good; yet to awaken them, stir them up, and soak them through and through, one must rely upon books of response and retribution. When one speaks to the people of today about goodness, none dares say it is wrong; yet toward books of response and retribution they are often unwilling to read them through, and some even knit their brows in displeasure. Judging their intent, it is likely they think the doctrine of response was made to teach wicked people, and since I am not wicked, why should I read it? I hold on the contrary that only a good person can read a good book. The reason is this: goodness responds to goodness as glue cast into lacquer, as butter blended with cream; things of kindred qi draw one another, and there is naturally a rich and savory flavor, so that day by day one advances and has merit. How true it is: only a good person can read good books, do good deeds, and set forth good teachings.

Yet I have something further to say. The Confucian and Daoist talk of response is like the Buddhist talk of cause and effect. Response is the cause; retribution is the effect. Therefore one who responds with goodness obtains the fruit of blessing; one who responds with unwholesomeness obtains the fruit of suffering; one who responds with the six pāramitās and the myriad practices and unsurpassed bodhi obtains the fruit of Buddhahood; one who responds with diligent cultivation of the Pure Land, reciting the Buddha’s name and seeking rebirth, obtains the fruit of the lotus terrace of Ultimate Bliss. There is no response that is not a cause, and no retribution that is not an effect. Once response is clear, cause and effect shine forth the more. All dharmas of the world and beyond the world can take this book as their ladder and stair. I only pray that every household keep a copy, believe, receive, and practice it, so that good thoughts daily increase and the mind-ground grows daily pure, and by dedicating this toward the Pure Land and seeking rebirth in Ultimate Bliss, one may draw near to the fruit of Buddhahood without difficulty. Is that not a great joy for those who reprint this book? This is the preface.
Third month of the bingshen year of the Guangxu reign, Qing dynasty
Respectfully recorded with washed hands by Zhang Bingyan, the Great Lotus Layman
