blocks.text: The Original Text of the Taishang Record of Responses and Retribution

inline.s: Taishang said: “Calamity and blessing have no gate; man brings them on himself. The recompense of good and evil follows like a shadow.”

Therefore Heaven and Earth have gods who oversee transgressions, and according to the lightness or heaviness of a man’s offenses they deduct from his span. When his span is diminished, he grows poor and wasteful, and often meets with care and trouble; all men hate him, punishments and calamities follow him, auspicious celebrations avoid him, and evil stars bring him disaster. When his span is exhausted, he dies.

There are also the spirit lords of the Three Terraces and the Northern Dipper, who dwell above a man’s head, record his crimes and evils, and deduct from his years and span. There are also the three corpse-spirits, who dwell within a man’s body; on every gengshen day they ascend to the heavenly bureau and report a man’s faults. On the last day of the month the hearth god does the same. Whenever a man commits a fault, for a great one his years are deducted, for a small one his span. The faults, great and small, number several hundred; one who seeks long life must first avoid them.

Advance along the Way; retreat from what is not the Way. Do not tread the crooked path; do not deceive in a dark room. Accumulate virtue and pile up merit; keep a compassionate heart toward all beings. Be loyal and filial, friendly and fraternal; rectify yourself and transform others. Pity the orphan and relieve the widow; honor the aged and cherish the young. Even insects, grasses, and trees must not be injured. One should pity the misfortune of others and delight in their goodness. Relieve others in their urgency; rescue them in their peril. Regard another’s gain as your own gain; regard another’s loss as your own loss. Do not expose another’s shortcomings; do not flaunt your own strengths. Halt evil and spread good; yield the greater and take the lesser. When insulted, do not resent it; when favored, be as one startled. Bestow kindness without seeking return; give to others without regret.

Such a one is called a good person. All men respect him; the way of Heaven protects him; blessing and emolument follow him; all wickedness departs from him; the spirits guard him. Whatever he undertakes must succeed, and immortality may be hoped for. One who seeks to be a celestial immortal should establish thirteen hundred good deeds; one who seeks to be an earthly immortal should establish three hundred good deeds.

But if one acts contrary to righteousness and walks against reason; if one counts evil as ability and bears to do cruelty and harm; if one secretly injures the good and honest, and in the dark insults one’s ruler and parents; if one is disrespectful to one’s teacher and betrays those one serves; if one deceives the ignorant and slanders one’s fellow students; if one is false, accusing, and fraudulent, and attacks one’s own clan and kin; if one is hard and unkind, fierce and self-willed; if one judges right and wrong improperly, and favors and opposes contrary to what is fitting; if one oppresses subordinates to seize merit and flatters superiors to court their will; if one receives kindness without gratitude and nurses resentment without end —

if one treats the people of Heaven with contempt and throws the affairs of state into disorder; if one rewards what is unrighteous and punishes the innocent; if one kills men to seize their wealth and overthrows others to seize their place; if one slaughters those who surrender and puts to death those who submit; if one demeans the upright and pushes aside the worthy; if one bullies the orphan and presses the widow; if one casts aside the law and takes bribes; if one calls the straight crooked and the crooked straight; if one makes light offenses heavy and adds wrath to those already condemned; if one knows a fault and does not change it, and knows the good and does not do it; if one shifts one’s own guilt onto others and blocks the proper arts; if one slanders the sages and worthy and encroaches upon the Way and its virtue —

if one shoots the flying and hunts the running, rouses the hibernating and startles the nesting; if one fills in burrows and overturns nests, injures the unborn and breaks eggs; if one wishes others to fail and ruins their success; if one endangers others to secure oneself and lessens others to benefit oneself; if one trades evil for good and private interest for public good; if one steals another’s ability and obscures another’s goodness; if one displays another’s ugliness and exposes another’s secrets; if one drains another’s goods and wealth and severs flesh and bone; if one encroaches on what others love and helps others do wrong; if one gives free rein to will and assumes authority, and humiliates others to win; if one ruins another’s crops and breaks up another’s marriage —

if one is arrogant in wealth and shameless in escaping blame; if one claims credit for kindness and shifts off fault, foists calamity on others and sells out the wicked; if one buys empty reputation and harbors a treacherous heart; if one thwarts another’s strength and shields one’s own weakness; if one uses power to coerce and lets loose violence to kill and wound; if one cuts and tailors without cause and butchers and cooks against propriety; if one scatters and wastes the five grains and troubles the multitude of living beings; if one wrecks another’s household and takes its goods and treasures; if one breaches dikes and sets fires to harm people’s dwellings; if one throws regulations into confusion to ruin another’s work; if one damages another’s implements and vessels to exhaust his use of them —

Seeing another honored and noble, one wishes him exiled and demoted. Seeing another wealthy, one wishes him broken and scattered. Seeing another beautiful, one rouses a private desire for her. Having wronged another over goods and wealth, one wishes him dead. When a request is not granted, one at once gives way to cursing and hatred. Seeing another meet with misfortune, one at once speaks of his faults. Seeing another’s body or features incomplete, one laughs at him; seeing another’s ability worthy of praise, one suppresses it.

To bury charms and curses to afflict others; to use poison to kill trees; to rage at one’s teacher and offend against father and elder brother; to take by force and demand by force, delighting in encroachment and seizure; to grow rich by plunder and seek promotion by cunning fraud; to be unfair in reward and punishment and immoderate in ease and pleasure; to be harsh and cruel to one’s subordinates and intimidate others; to resent Heaven and blame men, to curse the wind and scold the rain; to stir up quarrels and litigation and recklessly pursue factions; to follow the words of wife and concubines and disobey the instructions of father and mother; to forget the old when one gets the new, the mouth saying one thing and the heart another; to be greedy and grasping after wealth and to cheat and deceive one’s superiors; to fabricate evil words and slander and ruin the innocent; to destroy others and call it uprightness, to revile the gods and call it correctness; to cast aside obedience and imitate rebellion, to turn from kin and incline to strangers; to point to Heaven and Earth to attest one’s petty feelings, and to invoke the spirits to witness one’s sordid affairs —

To give and then regret it; to borrow and not repay. To scheme and seek beyond one’s portion; to lay burdens upon those below. To be excessive in lust, venomous in heart though kindly in face. To feed people with filthy food and delude the crowd with heterodox ways. To use short foot-rules and narrow measures, light scales and small pints. To mix the false in with the true and reap iniquitous profit. To press the good into lowliness and to insult and deceive the foolish. To be insatiably greedy and to invoke curses to prove oneself right.

To be addicted to wine and disorderly, so that flesh and bone quarrel in anger. Men unfaithful and unkind, women ungentle and uncompliant. Not in harmony with one’s wife; not respectful to one’s husband. Ever fond of boasting and given to jealousy. Without proper conduct toward wife and children; wanting in courtesy toward parents-in-law. To slight and neglect the spirits of the departed and to disobey the commands of superiors. To do what is of no benefit and to harbor an outward heart. To curse oneself and curse others; to show partial hatred and partial love. To step over wells and hearths; to leap over food and over people. To injure the unborn and procure abortion; to practice much that is secret and dark. To sing and dance on the last day of the month and on the winter sacrifice; to wail and rage on the first day of the month. To spit, blow the nose, and urinate facing north; to chant and weep facing the hearth. To light incense with the hearth fire and to cook food with filthy firewood. To rise at night and go naked; to carry out executions on the eight festival days. To spit at shooting stars and point at rainbows. To point at the three luminaries at will and to stare long at the sun and moon. To burn the fields and hunt in the spring months; to curse vilely facing north; to kill turtles and strike snakes without cause.

For sins such as these, the Director of Destinies deducts from a man’s years and span according to their lightness or heaviness. When his span is exhausted he dies. If death leaves a debt of guilt unpaid, then calamity reaches his descendants.

Again: those who seize the wealth of others by force — the reckoning is made against their wife and children and household, until death and mourning come upon them. If death and mourning do not come, then fire and flood, robbers and thieves, lost and ruined goods, illness and slanderous tongues and the like come upon them, to match the value of what they wrongfully took.

Again: those who kill men unjustly are in truth exchanging the sword and spear to slay one another. Those who take wealth that is not righteously theirs are like one who saves his hunger with tainted meat or quenches his thirst with poisoned wine. It is not that he is not briefly filled, but death too comes upon him.

When the heart stirs toward good, though the good is not yet done, auspicious spirits already follow it. When the heart stirs toward evil, though the evil is not yet done, inauspicious spirits already follow it. But one who has formerly done evil, and afterward repents and mends, who does no evil at all and practices every good, will in time surely obtain auspicious celebration. This is what is meant by turning calamity into blessing. Therefore the auspicious man whose speech is good, whose sight is good, and whose action is good has three goods in a day, and in three years Heaven will surely send down blessing upon him. The inauspicious man whose speech is evil, whose sight is evil, and whose action is evil has three evils in a day, and in three years Heaven will surely send down calamity upon him. Why then does one not strive and practice it?

blocks.text: A Compendium of Commentaries, Lectures, and Case Records on the Taishang Record of Responses and Retribution (Volume One)

inline.s: 1. Taishang said: Calamity and blessing have no gate; man brings them on himself.
2. The recompense of good and evil follows like a shadow.
3. Therefore Heaven and Earth have gods who oversee transgressions, and according to the lightness or heaviness of a man’s offenses they deduct from his span.
4. When his span is diminished he grows poor and wasteful, and often meets with care and trouble.
5. All men hate him.
6. Punishments and calamities follow him.
7. Auspicious celebrations avoid him.
8. Evil stars bring him disaster.
9. When his span is exhausted he dies.
10. There are also the spirit lords of the Three Terraces and the Northern Dipper, who dwell above a man’s head, record his crimes and evils, and deduct from his years and span.
11. There are also the three corpse-spirits, who dwell within a man’s body; on every gengshen day they ascend to the heavenly bureau and report a man’s faults.
12. On the last day of the month the hearth god does the same.
13. Whenever a man commits a fault, for a great one his years are deducted, for a small one his span.
14. The faults, great and small, number several hundred; one who seeks long life must first avoid them.
15. Advance along the Way; retreat from what is not the Way.
16. Do not tread the crooked path; do not deceive in a dark room.
17. Accumulate virtue and pile up merit.
18. Keep a compassionate heart toward all beings.
19. Loyalty and filial piety.

Taishang is a title of supreme honor. It means that he established his teaching in the name of Heaven, to show men that it must not be treated lightly. Response is like planting and sowing; retribution is like flower and fruit. Naming the treatise after these two words means that where there is response there must be retribution, and that retribution follows the response at once. It makes manifest the principle that the way of Heaven loves to return what is given. As the saying goes: Plant melons and you get melons, plant beans and you get beans. The net of Heaven is vast, and though its mesh is wide, nothing slips through. Is this not a saying about response?

The whole treatise takes its main thread from the first four lines, which already embrace the meaning of the entire work; everything that follows unfolds these four sayings. From “Therefore Heaven and Earth have gods who oversee transgressions” down to “one who seeks long life must first avoid them” is a general account of how closely the spirits watch and how severe the punishments are, first awakening in men a heart of awe and reverence. From “Advance along the Way” down to “should establish three hundred good deeds” speaks of the recompense by which doing good summons blessing. From “But if one acts contrary to righteousness” down to “calamity reaches his descendants” speaks of the recompense by which doing evil summons calamity. Below this, the two matters of seizing by force and killing unjustly are singled out for special emphasis, to show that these evils are especially grave.

From “When the heart stirs toward good” down to “inauspicious spirits already follow it” traces the matter further back to the first stirring of a thought, which the spirits already observe: the foundation of blessing and the embryo of calamity should be discerned with trembling care at the very outset. From “But one who has formerly done evil” down to “turning calamity into blessing” shows that one should not give oneself up because of past faults. If one can truly mend one’s faults and turn toward good, then calamity is turned into blessing, and in truth this is most easy. This is the fundamental intent of Taishang’s teaching, the meaning of the saying that calamity and blessing are in every case sought by oneself, which answers the earlier words that man brings them on himself. At the end it sums up with the three matters of speech, sight, and action as the rule and measure for practicing and accumulating good, and closes with an exhortation to strive. The single word strive is the essential key to mending faults and turning toward good. The earnestness of the admonition is deep and complete.

The ways of the world are no longer ancient, and men’s hearts are thin and watery. Rites and teachings cannot exhort and transform; punishments and penalties cannot restrain. Only the two words response and retribution can stir the conscience that turns men from evil toward good. Though men may not fear the king’s law, there is none who does not fear the spirits. From the king’s law one may sometimes escape by power or by cunning; but the spirits will surely not let a man go because he is rich, honored, or hidden away. Therefore one who wrote a preface to this treatise said: The good, hearing it, are the more encouraged, and do not wait for rewards to be added; the wicked, seeing it, are frightened for themselves, and fear that punishment will reach them. From this it is clear that this treatise not only supports the sacred scriptures but also assists the king’s transforming influence.

Men say that this treatise comes from the Daoist canon, and so suspect that it conflicts with Confucianism. This is always because they have never thoroughly studied the Confucian books. The Book of Changes says: The family that piles up goodness will surely have abundant blessing; the family that piles up unwholesomeness will surely have abundant calamity. Piling up shows that good and evil are never a single matter; abundant shows that the fruits of recompense are never of a single kind. The Commentary on the Changes states it in summary; this book sets it out item by item. Again, the Book of Documents records: Do good, and a hundred auspicious things are sent down upon you; do evil, and a hundred calamities are sent down upon you. The Book of Songs sings of how the Lord on high observes and beholds; the Record of Rites sets down the gain and loss of human affairs; the Spring and Autumn Annals show the event first and write the recompense after. The subtle sayings on response recorded in the Six Classics — how could they ever fail to agree with this in principle?

The good and evil recorded in this treatise are complete down to the finest detail; even spitting, coughing, singing, and weeping are all said to bear upon Heaven’s watching. Reading such words, men all suspect them to be vague and indistinct, impossible to pin down. They do not know that the way of being careful in small matters and cautious in subtle ones is precisely what the sages and worthies prized. The Book of Documents says: If one is not careful in small conduct, it will burden great virtue. The Book of Changes says: The petty man thinks a small good of no benefit and so does not do it, and thinks a small evil of no harm and so does not remove it; thus his evil piles up until it cannot be concealed, and his guilt grows great until it cannot be untied. In the whole Record of Rites, every single movement and action of a man has its rule and measure. When the ancients taught men to be careful in small matters and cautious in subtle ones, it was mostly like this.

Wang Zhijian, a presented scholar of Kunshan in the Ming dynasty, said: He read widely in all books and was versed also in the inner scriptures. He once told his disciples: The Record of Responses has two hundred ninety-three sayings, and within one treatise shallow and deep, coarse and fine, appear in turn. Take the one precept against killing. It says, “Even insects, grasses, and trees must not be injured” — that is exceedingly fine. It says, “butchers and cooks against propriety,” which does not forbid eating meat. It says, “cuts and tailors without cause,” which does not forbid wearing silk. Again it says, “burns the fields and hunts in the spring months,” and “kills turtles and strikes snakes without cause” — these seem all the more to broaden the path for men. The reason is that one is spoken for those who cultivate the Way, and one for those of ordinary custom. The person who cultivates the Way, having grasped its teaching and sought out its refinements, can transcend the ordinary and enter sagehood; while the person of ordinary habit and karma can also remove what is excessive in himself, and not come to have no dike or defense at all. This treatise must be read in this way, and then one knows that it does not repeat itself.

One who upholds this treatise must at every moment recite it silently in the mind, so that every word turns back into one’s own person: Have I this fault or not? Gradually let them grow few. Day after day thus, year after year thus, and naturally wherever one moves there is good, wherever one touches there is good. Other editions carry at the head of the volume rules for upholding and reciting, together with the various holy names; their meaning is simply to teach men to gather in the mind for the sake of goodness. One may follow the old example of Zhao Yuedao, who burned incense and reported to Heaven. But if one does not practice it in earnest and falls into the notion of reciting for blessings, then one has gone far astray.

This treatise speaks solely of the cultivation or perversion of the human heart. The Confucian teaching has the principle that virtue brings auspiciousness and defiance brings misfortune, and by this it becomes doubly clear. The Buddhist teaching has the doctrine of cause and effect and the round of rebirth, and by this its outline may be seen. The three teachings are one thread; different in form, alike in effect. Truly it is the stair to transcending the ordinary and entering sagehood, and the very road that turns calamity into blessing. I exhort all people alike to believe, receive, and practice it. The cases of its efficacy are set out below.

Wang Xiang, magistrate of Emei in the Southern Song, in the thirty-first year of the Shaoxing era made a vow to practice several dozen of the deeds in this treatise. One day he fell unconscious from illness, and his sons and daughters wept around him. Wang Xiang felt his body to be in mid-air, and heard the sound of weeping fine as bees or flies. After a little while a spirit said: Wang Xiang has just now wished to practice the Record of Responses with all his strength; he should quickly be sent back. Afterward he lived to the age of one hundred two.

Zhou Chi of Suining prefecture in the Southern Song recited this treatise daily and also loved to expound it to others. In mid-spring of the twenty-first year of Shaoxing he died suddenly, and after a day came back to life. He told his wife: I went to the realm of darkness and saw on either side only the starving dead of our district. An official on the hall called me and instructed me, saying: You were originally entered in the register of famine, but because you reverently upheld the Record of Responses and expounded and exhorted others, and because many who heard it turned their hearts and practiced good, your emolument and lifespan have now been altered. If you hold to the practice more firmly still, you may realize the great Way, and you will not come here again. Going out, he met a clerk who warned him: When you return to the world of the living, you should spread this treatise far and wide. If one region receives and upholds it, that region escapes calamity; if all under Heaven receives and upholds it, all under Heaven will be rich and well governed. Those who transmit it and those who uphold it alike have merit that is no small thing. Not only does it free one from the misfortunes of flood and fire, weapons and robbers, illness and disease — the seeking of heirs, of long life, of emolument, and of immortality all lie in this scripture.

Yang Shouye of Hejian in the Ming dynasty recited this treatise daily. At sixty he had no son. In the sixth year of Wanli he died of illness and suddenly came back to life. He told his family: In the darkness I saw an official holding a register and calling the roll. He said I had no son, but because I constantly recited the Record of Responses, my emolument and lifespan should be increased and a son granted me. The next year a boy was indeed born, who supported him in his old age and buried him at his death, and who in time passed the examinations.

Li Changling of Western Shu in the Song dynasty was prefect of Guangzhou. He redressed unjust cases and won a great reputation for his achievements. He wrote a detailed commentary on the Taishang Record of Responses, causing men to seek the principle through the matter and thereby aiding the spread of the teaching. The essential meaning of this scripture thus came to shine clearly in the world. He rose in office to vice censor-in-chief, and enjoyed both blessing and long life.

Zheng Qingzhi of Yue in the Song dynasty once presented this treatise to Emperor Lizong. After the emperor ascended the throne he granted money for its printing, and in his own hand wrote the two sayings “Do no evil at all; practice every good” at the head of the volume. From that time those who practiced it grew ever more numerous. Qingzhi had once promised to compose a eulogy but had not finished it; because of an eye ailment he forced himself to write the eulogy despite his illness, and his eyes at once recovered. Afterward he took part in the great administration and became associate director of the Bureau of Military Affairs.

Wang Zhu of Taizhou had a son named Jing, who died of illness at the age of four. In the depth of his grief he made a vow to print this treatise, wishing to have the dead boy as his son again, and his wife indeed conceived. When she went to Huangyan to offer incense, it seemed to her in a daze that she rode home in the same sedan chair as Jing, and she then gave birth to a son. He was named Shihui, and his face was no different from before. Flesh and bone were made whole again.

Yang Chen of Huangyan county saw others printing this treatise. Thinking that he himself had no means, he contributed as his karma allowed to the carving of one block, number seventeen. He dreamed that a spirit said: You have passed the examination exactly as you carved. And indeed he passed as the seventeenth jinshi.

Shen Qiu of Nanzhi, because his wife of the Xiang family was often ill during her pregnancy, made a vow to print a small volume so that people might uphold and recite it. On the day the workmen brought the blocks to his house, his wife gave birth to a boy, and mother and child were both blessed.

Wang Jingxu of Hangzhou wished to carve blocks and distribute them widely, but because of his humble office did not accomplish it. His son Yuan carried forward his father’s purpose, donated his property, and completed the carving, and sought contributions far and wide. Good men such as Shu and others printed and distributed ten thousand copies. Yuan dreamed that his father said to him: You have well completed my purpose, exhorting to goodness and distributing together with others. I have already been born in Heaven; your mother too has long life; and you and the others are named in the registers of the good.

Wang Xun of Jianzhou, long dead of illness, came to the courts of the dead, where he saw a government office whose plaque in gold letters read: Eastern Peak Prefecture. To the left of the hall stood a stele of gold letters, and it was the Record of Responses. Xun read it once through with joy and reverence, and at once heard a spirit say: Wang Xun, at the first sight of the true scripture, has given rise to such reverence and admiration. If he can practice it from now on and also keep the precept against killing, his illness will of itself be cured and his body at peace; there is no need for him to remain here. He thus came back to life, and his grave illness was at once healed. From this he practiced it without slackening. Now, an illiterate man reciting scripture is better than a literate one, because he has no random thoughts; and reciting from memory is better than reciting from a text, because it can gather in the mind. The essential point lies in the single word reverence. Wang Xun is proof of it.

Qin San of Cixi supported his mother in bitter poverty. Long ill and crippled, he met a Daoist who said: Follow me, and I will heal you. He then rubbed Qin San’s feet and he was at once cured. San told his mother and followed the man. The Daoist had San close his eyes, took him under the arm, and rode the wind until they came to a mountain on the sea. The mountain people exclaimed in surprise: This one has no immortal bones; how has he come here? The Daoist said: His family has made offerings to the Record of Responses for several generations and has always expounded and exhorted their descendants, so that the root of goodness has not been cut off. That is why I took him. San’s longing for his mother was urgent, and so he was carried back again. Thirteen days had passed.

The Daoist Zhang of Tianpeng recited the Record of Responses and lived by begging for alms. Yet he could recite only half of it. Suddenly he fell ill and came to the realm of darkness, where an official asked him: You recite the Record of Responses; why have you not mastered the whole text, but recite only half? You should return to the human world and undergo a hundred days of hardship. Going out, he met a clerk who warned him: Because you did not recite the whole text, you have come to this. Now you may repent and also exhort all people. Not only will you escape guilt, but your merit will increase. When the Daoist revived he told everyone in the region, and the people indeed came to revere and believe. That place had abundant harvests year after year, and the Daoist too recovered from his illness. Afterward he attained the Way.

Wang Yuan of Qiantang was poor and had no son, and only his aged mother remained at home. He recited this treatise daily and solicited funds to print and distribute it, praying for his mother’s long life and for an heir. When the first volume was carved his wife was already with child; afterward a son was born, and his mother enjoyed great age. Wang Yuan once said: By the sincerity of a single thought of mine, I sought long life for my mother and at once she had long life; I sought an heir and obtained an heir. The principle of response is indeed brightly clear.

Xu Tingyu of Hangzhou had a whole household that reverently upheld this treatise, and they wrote out a scroll of it and hung it in the hall. One night great robbers broke in to plunder, but it was as though something drove them out and they fled. Xu afterward learned the reason, and practiced it the more firmly.

Chen Bisong of Wulin was always one to aid others and benefit beings, and he carefully printed this treatise to circulate it throughout the seas and the world. It happened that rain fell for months on end, and a distant traveler had not returned. His wife kept watch at night without sleeping, when suddenly she heard a loud knocking at the door. At that time great robbers were plundering the neighborhood in succession, and every household was on strict guard. She started up thinking the robbers had come, and urgently called the family to flee together. They had just left the house when the high wall suddenly collapsed and the house and its vessels and goods were smashed to powder. The whole family came through without harm.

Zhou Rudeng of Haimen in the Ming dynasty attended Master Longxi’s lecture seat for years without gaining anything. Afterward he practiced this treatise and wrote a compendium of selections to exhort the world, and many turned toward good. By this merit, one day his mind-ground opened clear and he saw through to the sage Way, becoming a great Confucian of the late Ming. Alas, today Confucians study to be sages, Buddhists study to be Buddhas, and Daoists study to be immortals, yet some never awaken in a lifetime and some give up halfway. This is because their faculties are poor and they have no merit to give others. Zhang Ziyang said: Unless one accumulates practice and cultivates hidden virtue, at every turn a host of demons will make obstructive conditions. Can one who has set his will on the Way fail to rouse himself sharply?

Yu Yubi of Qiantang in the Ming dynasty had a wife of the Liang family who was afflicted by a haunting for three years. One night she dreamed that the Great Being Fayun descended amid the clouds, his radiance blazing, and all the ghosts and devils fled. The next day she paid reverence to Master Yunqi. Lady Liang reverently beheld his compassionate countenance, exactly as in her dream, and without knowing it felt a leap of joy, and her deep illness was at once healed. The master instructed her: Illness is born of karma, and karma is born of the mind. To practice merit with all one’s strength can prolong one’s years. He then gave Yu Yubi the Record of Responses, saying: Do no evil at all; practice every good — this in truth is the essential purport of the whole treatise. Spoken in shallow terms, to halt evil and spread good is only what a good commoner of a three-household village who keeps his place can do. Spoken in the fullest terms, to purify the least desire and perfect all good, to be the Heaven of heavens and the Sage of sages — the World-Honored One is no different from this. You should spread it widely to broaden the gift of Dharma. Yu Yubi was awakened, believed, and received it, and compiled eight volumes of Biaoyuan to exhort the world.

Fang Shike of Xiuning was sickly from childhood. He met a man of extraordinary powers who said: By your features you should be poor, and have neither son nor long life; you must plant many roots of goodness. He therefore made a vow to print this treatise and distribute it in exhortation. Afterward his illness was at once healed, his family gradually grew prosperous, and he had three sons, all honored, and died at a ripe age.

Mao Qizong of the Ming dynasty entered school to study in the bingwu year of Wanli. Whenever he had a little leisure he reverently recited this treatise. In the wuwu year he passed the provincial examination. In that examination he was close to death from illness, and when he entered the examination hall his four limbs were weary, his eyes could not see the ruled lines of the paper, and he did not know where to set his brush. After leaving the hall he could not remember a single word of what he had written. When he had passed, he saw his original paper, every character upright and regular, and only then knew that in the hall he had been aided by a spirit. In the jiwei year he failed, and again made a vow to expand his commentary on the Record of Responses, drawing widely on other sources and searching on every side, until nothing was left unexamined. When the book was finished he at once passed the jinshi examination, and rose in office to provincial administrator.

In the twelfth month of the jiashen year of Shunzhi in the Qing dynasty there was a great fire at Changmen in Suzhou. Three days beforehand someone was seen measuring the ground with a rod. The crowd asked him about it, and he answered with evasive words. Presently the fire burned exactly the area he had measured, fitting the boundaries he had marked, and men then realized it was a spirit. When the fire was burning, in Zhuanzhu Lane at Changmen there was a house belonging to Chen Songxuan in which a Xin’an merchant was lodging, no more than a foot from the flames. People on the city wall all saw a spirit standing on the roof, urgently rescuing it. After some time everything to left and right was destroyed, and this house alone remained. The next day they learned that the printing blocks of the Record of Responses carved by a Xin’an merchant were stored there.

Lu Zijin was a licensed student of Kuaiji who reverently upheld this treatise and annotated it in detail. Though his family was poor, he sold his rice fields to print and circulate it. His son Desheng rose in office to corrector in the Hanlin Academy.

The proofs of response recorded in past and present cannot all be told. I have here briefly set out the cases above, all of them firmly based on what has been seen and heard, trustworthy and conspicuous, to demonstrate the fixed principle of response. I only pray that those who take up this book will not treat it lightly. They should sit quietly and upright, put aside the floating breath, and hold a heart of reverence and humble receptivity, reading it carefully and in detail, savoring it deeply and practicing it with effort. This is a great good affinity; be careful not to lose it of yourself. How could I do more than burn incense and bow in earnest entreaty?

The Record of Auspicious Guidance says: First, awaken a heart of faith. That auspiciousness follows good and misfortune follows defiance, the sages have already stated decisively; yet the world points to the few cases where compliance and defiance do not quite match, and in its stupidity does not believe, saying that doing good does not necessarily bring recompense and doing evil does not necessarily bring calamity. This cuts off one’s own seeds of blessing and destroys the good roots of others. What manner of heart is this? One who sees this should rightly rouse a great faith. A single thought of faith is a single thought of good root; faith in every thought is good root in every thought.

Second, enjoin diligent practice. Now no one who does good with a wavering mind ever obtains recompense. To use one cup of water to save a whole cartload of firewood, and then to say that good need not be done, while sloth and carelessness rise up again — is that not to join the company of those who are deeply without benevolence? One should press hard at the practice, valiant and unremitting, always as though Heaven and Earth were facing me and the spirits were instructing me. Only thus does one not betray this body. Otherwise, drifting and heedless, day after day, how long is a human life? If I wait to accumulate slowly, I fear the impermanent will come suddenly, and then what use is regret?

Third, value the nourishing of the mind. Guanzi says: A joyful air meeting others is closer than brothers; an angry air meeting others is more cruel than weapons. The Nanhua too says: No weapon is more cruel than the will, and even the Moye sword ranks below it. From this we see that between will and air, before anything has been done for others, the containing of harmony and the drinking of richness is already as swift as a drum answering the stick. In ancient times Yu and Ji assisted Yao and Shun in settling the world: they brought those amid the waters to dwell on dry land, and brought the hungry to fullness. Truly their merit was vast and it truly reached the people. Yet the cloth-robed man of Mount Ni unfolded not a single plan — what did his empty words accomplish? Only that heart which sought the old in peace and the young in embrace, laboring earnestly until death, was in the end able to match in merit and equal in virtue those who faced south as rulers, and to be enshrined as teacher for ten thousand generations. Thus the mind contains all dharmas. If a man can but nourish the source, gentle and harmonious, lively and alert, not stirring the floating breath, then meeting kin he can be filial, meeting beings he can be kind, meeting good he can be decisive, meeting insult he can be patient. With the sentient and the insentient, in matter and in no matter, it is all one mass of living intent, filling the realm of space. How then can its blessing and virtue be conceived? This is the first and most urgent task of doing good.

Fourth, prize firmness and endurance. Small good brings near recompense; great good brings distant recompense. Near recompense is light in blessing; distant recompense is heavy in blessing. The substance of the willow and the cattail sprouts in a morning when planted in the evening; the pine and cypress are not so. They are hemmed in by weeds and thwarted by cattle and sheep, and only afterward is their use of a thousand or ten thousand years obtained. Among those of this world who have faith in goodness there is indeed no lack of men, but those who are firm and enduring are not often found. This is because, having practiced a few matters, and meeting with some setback by chance, they at once wrongly say that the way of Heaven is hard to know, and their former cultivation is suddenly cast aside — all misled by a heart that wants speed. Therefore one who piles up virtue though weak lays the foundation of blessing, and one who treads danger and holds firm shows the discernment of virtue. The ancients said: Plant virtue as though watering it; root out evil to the utmost. One often sees families that send up auspicious signs, some piling up practice over several generations, some striving at good for many years; the flowing of their abundant blessing is not a matter of morning to evening. If one has a small good fruit and at once hopes for thick blessing, then the root is already astray — by what means will blessing gather? Zhu Tianlin said: If one has a mind to move response, the response is not numinous; if one has a mind to pray for retribution, the retribution does not come. This should be left to the natural, and one must not recklessly conjecture. Therefore firmness and endurance are especially the pivot of piling up virtue.

Fifth, value transmission and circulation. Wherever the scriptures are, there is a good affinity. To hide them and not let them flow must bring heavenly calamity. The Ledger of Merits and Demerits holds that one who transmits a book of goodness to one person is credited with ten good deeds, to ten persons with a hundred good deeds, to a great noble, a great hero, or a person of great power with a thousand good deeds, and one who reprints and circulates it without limit with ten thousand good deeds. To praise it at every moment and remind men at every moment — so that even the farmer and the woman in the inner rooms, the herd-boy and the village child, are all transformed — good affinity is boundless and the affinity of blessing is boundless too. In ancient times Master Sun printed the Prescriptions Worth a Thousand in Gold, and when the book was finished he departed as an immortal. Zhou Chi expounded the Record of Responses to others and escaped the register of famine. How could the virtue of public goodness be measured?

Sixth, may others add and expand upon it. How many are the good and evil recompenses of past and present? How can the chance notes of a brush fully capture them all? Those who share this intent may take what they find in books and records, or what they obtain from sight and hearing, and it is no harm to continue adding to it. Bring a greater brush to bear, pick out the subtle and the perilous, and make it leap up before men’s eyes. A single phrase of praise is a single phrase that protects the root of goodness; a single thought that stirs a man is also a single thought that erases evil karma. The more brightly it is expounded, the more clearly the highest principle appears. To aid Heaven in unfolding the teaching — the merit is rich indeed.

This section, joined with the next, forms one main thread of the treatise: it is the great purport of the teaching handed down. As for the hearts of the sages and worthies, they did not do good and refrain from evil because they prayed for blessing and avoided calamity. As for the principle of creation, piling up good and piling up evil bring abundant blessing and abundant calamity, and this never fails.

In small terms it is called auspiciousness and inauspiciousness; in great terms, calamity and blessing. No gate means no fixed gate. Brings them on himself means that one does it and one receives it. It says that Heaven and Earth are without partiality, giving to each thing according to the thing itself. Calamity or blessing has originally no fixed gate; it awaits what a man summons to make its recompense. It lies only in the heart of man summoning it himself. Yet when a man’s single thought has not yet arisen, this mind is clear and still, like empty space — where is good or evil? Only because this thought has just stirred: where it turns to good matters, that is good; where it turns to bad matters, that is evil. At first it is no more than a single thought arising and a single matter done; but later, as days pile up and months accumulate, there comes to be the difference between a good man and a wicked man, and the obtaining of calamity or of blessing is decided entirely at the moment the thought arises. Therefore Taishang opens his mouth and says no gate, and says brings them on himself, trembling before the moment when a man’s thought arises, pressing him hard to arouse and awaken. To be awake is to look within and see clearly. In the human heart, good and evil always have their incipient moment. With one thought of inward illumination one knows where one is tending. The Book of Changes says: The incipient is the subtlety of movement, the first appearance of good fortune and misfortune. If one can see through at this point and be master there, then naturally desire is purified and principle made pure, and one’s movement meets with the auspicious. But if there is the least discrepancy, then Heaven and Earth are set worlds apart.

Chan Master Lingyuan of the Song dynasty said to Yichuan: Calamity can give birth to blessing, and blessing can give birth to calamity. That calamity can give birth to blessing is because when one is in danger one is urgent to think of safety, deep in seeking the principle, and especially able to be reverent, cautious, and careful. That blessing can give birth to calamity is because when one dwells in safety one gives free rein to luxurious thoughts and lets loose one’s pride and sloth, and is especially prone to carelessness and contempt.

The Great Emperor of the Eastern Peak instructed: Doing good is like the grass of a spring garden — you do not see it grow, yet it increases daily. Doing evil is like the whetstone of a knife — you do not see it wear, yet it diminishes daily. Calamity and blessing shift in secret, and the deluded never awaken.

Huineng, the Sixth Patriarch of the Tang dynasty, said: All fields of blessing are not apart from the square inch. The scripture says: Good fortune and misfortune, calamity and blessing, are all made by the mind. It also says: The two wheels of guilt and blessing and the two fruits of suffering and joy are all made by the three kinds of karma and sensed by the one mind. If a single thought of mind is anger and sexual misconduct, that is the karma of hell. If it is stinginess and greed and not giving, that is the karma of hungry ghosts. If it is folly and dull darkness, that is the karma of animals. If it is self-conceit and arrogance, that is the karma of asuras. If one firmly keeps the five precepts, that is the karma of humans. If one finely practices the ten good deeds, that is the karma of gods. If one realizes the emptiness of the person, that is the karma of śrāvakas. If one knows that conditions are by nature apart, that is the karma of pratyekabuddhas. If one cultivates the six pāramitās together, that is the karma of bodhisattvas. If one has true compassion and equanimity, that is the karma of Buddhas. Now when the mind is pure, there are the jeweled trees and the fragrant terrace, and one is born by transformation in a pure land. When the mind is defiled, there are the hills and the pits and hollows, and one receives birth in a filthied land. It is not sent down from Heaven, nor is it born of the earth; it comes about solely from the first single thought. Apart from the source of mind there is no other substance.

How subtle is the mechanism of response; how perilous the road of good and evil. What is hardest to hold and guard is the human heart. Touched by things it stirs, now sinking into the abyss, now flying to the heavens; following thoughts it shifts, now freezing to ice, now burning to fire. Therefore the ancients by day diligently examined themselves three times, and by night were watchful of the four knowings; and further, rising at cockcrow, they labored earnestly at good. All this was nothing but holding and preserving at every hour, so that this mirror of the mind should be constantly bright. When the mirror of the mind is bright, then one can be master of one’s own good and evil, and master of calamity and blessing too; the mandate of Heaven is indeed in me. Therefore in discussing the principle that calamity and blessing are summoned by oneself, one traces it back to the preserving of the mind. I append here the standard discourses of earlier Confucians, to unfold the purport of Taishang.
Someone asked: If one rises at cockcrow before one has contact with things, how does one do good? Master Cheng said: Simply to abide in reverence is to do good.

Master Zhang of the Song dynasty said: At the beginning of rectifying the mind, one should take one’s own mind as a stern teacher. In every movement one makes, one then knows fear. If for one or two years one holds this firmly, the mind will naturally be rectified.

Master Zhu said: Master Luo taught students, in quiet sitting, to observe what appearance the emotions of joy, anger, sorrow, and happiness present before they have arisen. This too is an essential of nourishing the mind.

He also said: The mind must be made to stay in one place only, with no outside matters mixed in, and one must still hold and guard it diligently, never relaxing for a moment when matters come. A man’s spirit, through long habit, forms itself. If one gathers it in with diligence and truly holds it tight, then even half a month may show proof.

He also said: The work of nourishing the source is the readiest of all to be interrupted. Yet the moment one becomes aware of the interruption is the very place where it is continued. One need only constantly arouse and remind oneself, accumulating little by little, and in time it will naturally continue and be beaten into one piece.

He also said: That private thoughts arise thickly in quiet is the common affliction of students. To be able to examine oneself to this point is very hard to attain. Here one should take reverence as the master, and deeply examine what matters the private thoughts chiefly sprout about; then, at the heaviest point, inflict sharp punishment and block them. In time, with mastery, proof will of itself appear. One must not reckon merit by morning and evening, nor multiply explanations to confuse it.
He also said: If the mind is preserved, the host of false thoughts naturally withdraws and obeys.

He also said: Confucius said: In dwelling, be respectful; in handling affairs, be reverent; with others, be loyal. This is the method of preserving the mind. If in speaking you feel a thing is wrong, then do not say it; if in doing you feel a thing is wrong, then do not do it. This too is the method of preserving the mind.

He also said: In learning one must rouse oneself and awaken. The monk Ruiyan used to ask himself every day: Is the master awake? And he would answer himself: Awake. Students should take this as their model.

His disciple Zhou Yanwen asked: Lately I feel that in walking and sitting, in speech and silence, I cannot deceive myself. Master Zhu said: This is the place where you have gained strength; the mind has come home to the body. Only keep silently recognizing it at every moment and preserving it.

Chen Lie of the Song dynasty suffered from a poor memory. Chancing to read Mencius — “The way of learning is nothing other than this: to seek the lost mind and that is all” — he suddenly awakened and said: My mind has never been gathered in; how could I remember? He then shut the door, sat quietly, and did not read for more than a hundred days, in order to gather in his lost mind. After that he read, and at one glance nothing was left behind.

Someone asked what reverence looks like. Xie Shangcai said: It can be seen in the time of solemn thoughtfulness. He asked: If one cannot avoid a certain stiffness, what then? He said: Stiffness carried too far is not right either. The point lies in neither forgetting nor forcing growth.

Gao Jingyi said: Whenever the sun sets, I silently examine what I have done through the day. If I have not truly tempered body and mind, then I have wasted a day, and the flowing light is to be feared. He also said: The reason one should cherish every inch of time is so that evil thoughts and false notions do not in an instant seize my spirit-house, and thus day by day and month by month one may advance, continuing bright toward the light. He also said: The earlier Confucians’ method of entering reverence is stated as orderly gravity, as constant awakeness, and as gathering in so that not one thing is admitted. Today our breasts are full of toil and clamor, and a thousand myriad things are all admitted here — how much more than one thing. To be free of this, one must be constantly awake. To be awake, one must be orderly and grave. And these three methods have their order.
Without desire, therefore still; with a master, therefore empty. This is the outline of the mind-learning.

Master Cheng Mingdao of the Song dynasty and his younger brother Yichuan were crossing the river when the boat nearly capsized. All the men were terrified, but the master alone sat upright and grave as usual. When asked about it, he said: The mind was preserved in sincerity and reverence, that is all.

The old monk of the True Emptiness Monastery said: Men’s false thoughts are not of one kind. Some recall events of several decades past — honor and disgrace, kindness and enmity, parting and reunion in sorrow and joy, and all manner of idle feelings: these are false thoughts of the past. Some, when a matter comes before them and could be met with compliance, instead fear the head and dread the tail, hesitating and unable to decide: these are false thoughts of the present. Some look forward to wealth and glory in days to come, to the advancement of sons and grandsons, and to all matters that cannot necessarily be achieved or necessarily obtained: these are false thoughts of the future. These three kinds of false thought arise and cease, and are called the illusory mind. To illumine and see through their falseness, and cut them off as each thought arises, is called the awakened mind. Therefore it is said: Do not fear the arising of thoughts; fear only that awakening comes late. If this mind is like the great void, where can affliction set its foot?

The above are all discourses of refined subtlety and spiritual transformation, upon which one who has set his will should deeply reflect and strive, until he arrives at mastery and naturalness and then stops. In former times Duke Zhao Kangjing of the Song dynasty set out two things, a bottle and beans: when a good thought arose he dropped in a white bean, and when an evil thought arose he dropped in a black bean. At first the black beans were very many, then they gradually grew few, and in time he forgot both good and evil thoughts, and the bottle and beans were cast aside unused — for he had worn them away to clarity and transparency. Again, the Wenchang Colophon on Hidden Virtue says: If a man can preserve his mind as I do, Heaven will surely grant you blessing. For the preserving of the mind lies with me; one need only seek to subdue the private and restore the nature in order to serve Heaven. As for Heaven’s recompense, things of kindred qi follow one another, and it never fails. From this we know that the way to remove calamity and summon blessing lies precisely in preserving the mind. How fine is this purport!

Wei Zhongda of the Song dynasty was at first a Hanlin official, and was taken to the realm of darkness, where the two registers of good and evil were examined. The register of evil filled the courtyard; the register of good was only one small scroll. The underworld official’s countenance changed, and he called for a scale to weigh them. The small scroll outweighed and lifted the register of evil. The official said with joy: You may leave. Zhongda said: I am not yet forty; how could I have such a quantity of evil? The official said: Whenever a single thought is not upright, the spirits know it without exception. Knowing it, they write it down; they do not wait for the deed. He asked: What is in the small scroll? The official said: The court once undertook a great labor, building the stone bridge of the Three Mountains. You remonstrated strongly against it; this is the draft of your memorial. He said: The remonstrance was not followed; how could the power of the good reach so far? The official said: Your thought was most sincere, and your words could instruct the world. Had they been followed, the merit would have been beyond measure, and by it the world might have been saved with no difficulty. But alas, your evil thoughts were too many, and the power of the good was halved; you cannot hope again for the great chancellorship. In the end his office stopped at minister of the Ministry of Personnel. Alas! Zhongda’s evil existed only as thoughts, and still it diminished the present blessing of becoming chancellor. Zhongda’s good existed only as words, and it outweighed a register of evil that filled the courtyard. How much more for one who actually does good and evil? From this it is clear that the place where a single thought arises is the gate of calamity and blessing.

Liao Deming of the Song dynasty was a disciple of Zhu Hui’an. In his youth he dreamed that he carried a calling card to visit a temple, and the gatekeeper asked for the card; he took it from his sleeve and it read: Liao, of the bureau of instruction. Then he woke. Afterward he passed the examinations, and indeed governed Fujian as a court gentleman of instruction. Deming thought of the former dream and feared his office would stop there, and did not wish to go. He therefore consulted Hui’an. The master pointed to things on his desk and said: Man and vessel are not the same. A brush can only be a brush, and a sword cannot become a zither; thus their completion or ruin, their duration or brevity, have a fixed number. Man is not so. There are indeed those who are a robber Zhi in the morning and a Shun by evening, and their good fortune and misfortune change accordingly; it is hard to speak of them in fixed terms. Now you are going to your post; you need only broaden and enlarge your virtue and practice good deeds with all your strength. The former dream is not worth a mustard seed of concern. Deming followed his words, and afterward his office indeed reached that of a full court gentleman.

Bi Chang’s family was wealthy, but he deceived others only by cunning and built his fortune by harshness and meanness. He had two sons. When someone wished to sell him land, he would refuse to his face, saying: I do not want it. Then he would send someone secretly to lure the seller; and when the man came, he would say again: I truly do not want it. The man, having no recourse, was forced to lower his price to make the sale; and when the contract was made he would say: My silver is not convenient; come to fetch it on a certain day. And when the man came to fetch it, he would pay partly in debased silver or make up the sum with grain, so that the original amount was never received in full. All his life every matter was like this. Afterward his elder son was imprisoned for a case of manslaughter, and died after the family was ruined; his younger son drifted into gambling and debauchery, and begged for food in distant parts; and Bi Chang himself came at last to have no heir at all.

Yuan Liaofan of the Ming dynasty wrote his own chapter on establishing destiny, saying: In my childhood I lost my father, and my mother bade me give up my studies and learn medicine, saying that it could nourish life and could aid others, and that to master one art and make a name by it had been my late father’s own wish. Later, at the Ciyun Monastery, I met an old man with a long beard and a grand bearing, floating as though he were an immortal. I bowed to him with respect. He said to me: You are a man destined for the road of office; next year you will enter the school. Why do you not study? I told him the reason. He said: My surname is Kong; I am from Yunnan. I received the orthodox transmission of Master Shao’s Supreme Principles, and the number prescribes that I should transmit it to you. I at once led him home and told my mother. We tested his calculations, and the finest details all proved true. I then roused the thought of studying. Kong cast my numbers for me: in the county examination for the young candidate I should be fourteenth; in the prefectural examination, seventy-first; in the examination of the education commissioner, ninth. The next year I went to the examinations, and the ranks in all three places matched. He then divined for me the good and ill of my whole life, saying that in a certain year I should rank thus and so, in a certain year be granted stipend, in a certain year become a tribute student, and in a certain year after that be selected as a great magistrate of Sichuan; that after three and a half years in office I should properly resign and return home; and that at the hour of the ox on the fourteenth day of the eighth month of my fifty-third year I should die in my own bed. He added with regret that I should have no son. I recorded it all fully and carefully kept it in mind. From then on, whenever I sat for an examination, the order and the ranks never fell outside what Master Kong had fixed in advance. Only he had reckoned that I should eat ninety-one piculs and five pecks of stipend rice before leaving as a tribute student; yet when I had eaten a little over seventy piculs, Master Tu, the commissioner, approved my promotion to tribute. I privately doubted it. Afterward it was indeed rejected by Master Yang, who held the seal in acting capacity, and only in the dingmao year was my tribute status approved; and counting the rice eaten before that, it came in truth to ninety-one piculs and five pecks. Because of this I believed the more firmly: advance and retreat have their destiny, and slowness and speed have their time. I became calm and sought nothing. As a tribute student I entered the capital at Yan, and stayed in the capital for a year, sitting quietly all day and not reading any writing.

Afterward I returned and traveled to the Southern Academy. Before entering the college, I first visited Chan Master Yungu in the Qixia Mountains. We sat facing each other in one room for three days and nights without closing our eyes. Yungu asked me: The reason ordinary men cannot become sages is only that idle thoughts entwine them. You have sat for three days and I have not seen a single idle thought arise. I said: Master Kong has calculated it all for me. Honor and disgrace, death and life, all have their fixed number; even if I wished to indulge in idle thoughts, there would be nothing to indulge in. Yungu laughed and said: I took you for a hero, but you are after all only an ordinary man. I asked him why. He said: A man cannot be without mind, and so he is bound by yin and yang; how could he be without a number? But only ordinary men have a number. For a man of the utmost goodness the number cannot hold him fast, and for a man of the utmost wickedness the number cannot hold him fast either. For twenty years you have been fixed by his calculations and have not stirred a hair’s breadth — is that not an ordinary man? I asked: Then can the number be escaped? He said: Destiny is made by myself; blessing is sought by myself. What the Songs and Documents declare is indeed clear instruction. In my own scriptures it is said: Seek official rank and you obtain official rank; seek wealth and honor and you obtain wealth and honor; seek sons and daughters and you obtain sons and daughters; seek long life and you obtain long life. Now false speech is a great precept of Śākyamuni; how could the Buddhas and bodhisattvas deceive men with false speech? I pressed further: Mencius says, “Seek it and you obtain it, for what is sought lies within me.” Virtue, the Way, benevolence, and righteousness can be sought with effort; but how can official rank and wealth and honor be obtained by seeking? Yungu said: Mencius’s words are not wrong; it is you who have misunderstood them. Have you not seen what the Sixth Patriarch says — all fields of blessing are not apart from the square inch; seek from the mind, and no response fails to penetrate. Seeking within myself, I obtain not only virtue, the Way, benevolence, and righteousness, but also official rank and wealth and honor: both within and without are gained. This is a seeking that benefits the gaining. But if one does not turn back and examine oneself within, and only gallops outward in pursuit, then although there is a way of seeking, the obtaining of it depends on destiny; both within and without are lost, and so it is of no benefit. He asked: What did Master Kong calculate for your whole life? I told him the truth. Yungu said: Consider for yourself whether you ought to obtain examination rank, and whether you ought to have sons. I reflected for a long while and said: I ought not. Those who hold examination rank are generally men of a fortunate countenance. My blessing is thin, and I have not been able to pile up merit and practice to lay a foundation for thick blessing. I have no patience for troublesome and vexatious affairs, and I cannot tolerate others. Sometimes I use my talent and cleverness to overshadow people; I speak and act bluntly; I am light and reckless in talk. All these are marks of thin blessing — how should I be fit for examination rank? Where the earth is foul, many things grow; where the water is clear, there are often no fish. I love cleanliness. Harmony can nourish the ten thousand things; I am given to anger. Love is the root of life upon life; endurance is the root of barrenness. I am jealous of my reputation and integrity, and constantly unable to give up myself to save others. And I talk overmuch and drain my qi; I delight in drink and burn away my essence; I love to sit through the whole night without knowing how to preserve the primal and nourish the spirit. All this means I ought to have no sons. My other faults and evils are still many and cannot be counted. Yungu said: How should it be only examination rank? In the world, one who enjoys a thousand in gold of property is surely a man of a thousand in gold; one who enjoys a hundred in gold of property is surely a man of a hundred in gold; one who ought to die of starvation is surely a man of starvation. Heaven does no more than strengthen each according to his material; when did it ever add the least intention of its own? Even as to having sons: one who has the virtue of a hundred generations will surely have descendants of a hundred generations to preserve it; one who has the virtue of ten generations will surely have descendants of ten generations to preserve it; one who has the virtue of three generations or two will surely have descendants of three or two generations to preserve it. And one whose line is cut off and has no posterity has virtue at its thinnest. Since you now know your faults, you should thoroughly change and scrub away the marks by which you failed to obtain examination rank and failed to have sons. You must pile up virtue; you must be tolerant; you must be harmonious and loving; you must cherish your essence and spirit. The many things of the past are like death yesterday; the many things hereafter are like birth today. This is the body reborn of principle and righteousness. Now the body of flesh and bone still has its number; how could the body of principle and righteousness fail to move Heaven? The Tai Jia says: Calamities sent by Heaven may yet be avoided; calamities one brings on oneself cannot be escaped. The Book of Songs says: Ever speak and match the mandate, and seek for yourself abundant blessing. If Master Kong calculated that you would not obtain examination rank and would not have sons, that is a calamity made by Heaven, and it may still be avoided. If you now practice good deeds with all your strength and pile up much hidden virtue, that is blessing made by yourself — how could you fail to receive and enjoy it? The Book of Changes plans for the gentleman, that he may pursue the auspicious and avoid the inauspicious. If the mandate of Heaven were fixed, how could the auspicious be pursued and the inauspicious avoided? Its very first principle in the opening chapter says: The family that piles up goodness will surely have abundant blessing; the family that piles up unwholesomeness will surely have abundant calamity. Can you believe this firmly enough? I believed his words, bowed, and received his teaching.

I therefore laid bare before the Buddha all the guilt of my former days, and wrote out a memorial. I first sought to pass the examinations, and vowed to practice three thousand good deeds, to repay the virtue of Heaven and Earth and of my ancestors. Yungu brought out the Ledger of Merits and Demerits and showed it to me, bidding me record each day the matters I had done: good deeds to be counted, evil deeds to be deducted. He also taught me to uphold the Cundi mantra, in the hope that it would surely prove efficacious. He said to me: The masters of talismans say that one who cannot write a talisman is laughed at by the ghosts and spirits. There is a secret transmission here: it is simply not stirring a thought. When you take up the brush to write a talisman, first lay down all conditions; then, from the place where the thought does not stir, set down one dot, which is called the opening of chaos. From there the whole talisman is written off in one stroke, with no further thought or deliberation, and the talisman is then numinous. In all praying to Heaven and establishing destiny, one must move response from the place of no thought and no deliberation. When Mencius discussed the learning of establishing destiny, he said that early death and long life are not two. Examined in detail: plenty and famine are not two, and then one may establish the destiny of poverty and wealth; adversity and success are not two, and then one may establish the destiny of honor and lowliness; early death and long life are not two, and then one may establish the destiny of death and life. In a man’s life in the world, only death and life are of weight; and if one speaks of early death and long life, then all compliance and defiance are included in it. As for cultivating oneself so as to await it, this is the matter of piling up virtue and praying to Heaven. Cultivate means that wherever there are faults and evils in the self, all should be dealt with and removed. Await means that the least covetous hope and the least greeting of what has not come should all be cut off. Arriving at this position, one goes straight to the realm before Heaven, and this very thing is true learning. You are not yet able to be without mind; but you can uphold the Cundi mantra, without keeping count and without number, never letting it be interrupted. When you uphold it to mastery, then in upholding there is no upholding, and in no upholding there is upholding. When you arrive at the point where the thought does not stir, then it will be efficacious.

My first style was Xuehai. On that day I changed it to Liaofan, for I had awakened to the teaching of establishing destiny and wished no longer to fall into the rut of the ordinary man. From then on I was cautious and trembling all day, and felt myself different from before. Formerly I had only drifted and let myself go; now I had of myself a scene of trembling fear and vigilant effort. In a dark room and in the hidden corner of a house I was constantly afraid of offending Heaven and Earth and the spirits. When men hated me or slandered me, I could of myself bear it calmly. By the next year, when the Ministry of Rites held the examination, Master Kong had calculated that I should be third; suddenly I was first. His words did not prove true, and in the autumn examination I passed. Yet my practice of righteousness was not yet pure, and my self-examination found many faults. Sometimes I saw a good deed and did it without courage; sometimes I saved others while my heart was constantly doubting itself; sometimes I forced my body to do good while my mouth spoke faults; sometimes I held myself in hand when awake and let myself go when drunk. Weighing faults against merits, my days were commonly spent in vain. From the year jisi, when I made my vow, until the year jimao, more than ten years passed, and only then were the three thousand good deeds complete. I then made the vow to seek a son, and also promised to practice three thousand good deeds. In the year xinsi a son was born, Tianqi. Each time I did a deed I at once noted it down. Your mother could not write, so for every deed she did she used a goose-feather tube to stamp a little circle on the calendar. Sometimes she gave to the poor, sometimes she released living creatures, and in one day there were sometimes more than ten circles. By the eighth month of the year guiwei the number of three thousand was complete. On the thirteenth day of the ninth month I again made the vow to pass the jinshi examination, promising to practice ten thousand good deeds. In the year bingxu I passed, and was appointed magistrate of Baodi. I prepared a blank book and named it the Record of Governing the Mind. When I rose in the morning and sat in the hall, my family brought it and gave it to the gate servant to place on my desk; whatever good or evil I did, down to the finest detail, was always recorded. At night I set a table in the courtyard and, following the old practice of Zhao Yuedao, burned incense and reported to Heaven. Your mother, seeing that few deeds were done, would knit her brows and say: Formerly at home I helped you do good, and so the three thousand were completed. Now you have vowed ten thousand, and there is nothing to be done in the office; when will the vow be fulfilled? At night I happened to dream of a spirit. I told him the reason why the good deeds were hard to complete. The spirit said: By the single matter of reducing the grain tax alone, the ten thousand deeds are all complete. Now the fields of Baodi were taxed at two fen, three li, and seven hao per mu. I made arrangements and reduced it to one fen, four li, and six hao. Since this matter had really happened, my heart was somewhat doubtful. Just then Chan Master Huanyu came from Mount Wutai. I told him the dream and asked whether the matter should be believed. The master said: If this mind is true and earnest, then a single deed can match ten thousand good deeds — how much more the reducing of the grain tax for a whole county, with ten thousand people receiving the blessing? I at once donated my salary and had him go to Mount Wutai to make an offering to ten thousand monks and dedicate the merit.
